descripcion_es: Finished time versus unfinished time; the time markers for each.
resumen: The past simple is used when the moment in the past is finished and is mentioned or understood; the present perfect, when the period continues up to now or when it does not matter when it happened.

explicacion.texto: The key is not whether the action happened “recently”, but whether the time we are referring to is closed. Unlike the Spanish of Spain, “Esta mañana he ido al banco” is I went to the bank this morning if the morning is already over.

cabecera: Present perfect (up to now / no date)
filas: yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago
when I was a child, on Monday
so far, recently, lately, since, for
Have you ever been to Rome?

items: Experience with no date: I've visited Japan twice. With a date: I visited Japan in 2018.
A conversation often starts in the present perfect and moves to the past simple when giving details: Have you seen the film? Yes, I saw it last Saturday.
Questions with When or What time always take the past simple: When did you buy it?
With today, this week, this year: present perfect if the period has not finished; past simple if it has finished or you are thinking of a specific moment.

explicacion.texto: Living or dead person: Shakespeare wrote many plays (his life is over); My sister has written two novels (she may write more).

ejemplos.frase: I've lost my keys. Can you help me look for them?
ejemplos.traduccion: He perdido las llaves. ¿Me ayudas a buscarlas?

ejemplos.frase: I lost my keys last week, but I found them the next day.
ejemplos.traduccion: Perdí las llaves la semana pasada, pero las encontré al día siguiente.

ejemplos.frase: Have you ever eaten octopus? — Yes, I ate it in Galicia.
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Has comido pulpo alguna vez? — Sí, lo comí en Galicia.

ejemplos.frase: He worked in London for five years, then moved to Dublin.
ejemplos.traduccion: Trabajó en Londres cinco años y luego se mudó a Dublín.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With a finished time reference (yesterday, ago, last…) use the past simple.
Questions with When ask for a specific moment: past simple.
A situation that started in the past and continues is expressed with the present perfect.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: with finished time expressions (yesterday, last week, two days ago) you use the past simple. The clue is last night: last night is already over, so the action is placed at a specific past moment. That is why it is watched. The present perfect cannot be combined with a finished time expression.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Last night is finished time: past simple.

por_opcion.have watched: Incorrect: the present perfect does not combine with a finished time like last night.
por_opcion.watched: Correct: past simple for an action at a specific, finished past moment.
por_opcion.have been watching: Incorrect: the present perfect continuous indicates something that continues up to now; it does not fit with last night.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the card about experience with no date: the question is about the person's whole life up to now, a period that has not finished. The clue is ever, which the table includes among the present perfect words. That is why the question starts with the auxiliary Have: Have you ever been to Canada? Note that been to means having gone somewhere and come back.

por_opcion.Did: Incorrect: did you ever been mixes two tenses; besides, for an experience in your whole life you use the present perfect. Did you ever go…? exists in American English, but with go, not with been.
por_opcion.Have: Correct: the present perfect auxiliary; with ever and been it forms the typical question about experience.
por_opcion.Were: Incorrect: were you ever been is not a possible form; were does not form tenses with the participle been.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the note in the card about living or dead people: when the subject has died, the period of their life is finished and you use the past simple (Shakespeare wrote many plays). The clue is the subject, Picasso, who can no longer paint any more works. That is why it is painted. If we were talking about a living painter, the present perfect (has painted) would indicate that their work is still open.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Picasso is dead: his life is a finished period.

por_opcion.has painted: Incorrect: the present perfect would imply that Picasso can still go on painting; his life is a finished period.
por_opcion.painted: Correct: past simple because Picasso's life is a closed period.
por_opcion.has been painting: Incorrect: the continuous form would indicate that he is still painting now, which is impossible.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: since goes with the present perfect because the period continues up to now. The clue is since 2010: the situation started then and continues today. That is why it is have lived, although Spanish uses the present “vivimos desde”. The past simple would suggest they no longer live there, and the present simple cannot go with since.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Since + a situation that continues today: present perfect.

por_opcion.lived: Incorrect: the past simple would suggest a closed period, and since 2010 indicates that it continues today.
por_opcion.have lived: Correct: present perfect for a situation that started in 2010 and continues.
por_opcion.live: Incorrect: calque of the Spanish present; with since English requires the present perfect.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the present perfect or the past simple.
ejercicios.frase: She ___ (buy) a new car two weeks ago.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the past simple table: two days ago is one of its examples. The clue is ago, which always marks a finished moment counted back from now. That is why the verb is in the past simple, and as buy is irregular, its past form is bought. The present perfect is never used with ago.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Ago marks a finished moment: past simple.
ejercicios.traduccion: Se compró un coche nuevo hace dos semanas.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Ago marks a specific past moment; the present perfect does not combine with it.
Buy is irregular: its past form is bought.
Ago is already in the sentence, after two weeks; only the verb goes in the gap.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the present perfect or the past simple.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the present perfect table: yet is one of its typical words. The clue is yet at the end of the negative sentence: it means “up to now” and refers to a period that is still open, since I can still finish it. That is why it is haven't finished (or have not finished). American English sometimes allows I didn't finish it yet, but standard and British English prefer the present perfect.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Yet in a negative sentence goes with the present perfect.
ejercicios.traduccion: Todavía no he terminado el informe.

errores_previstos.explicacion: With yet the standard form is the present perfect; the past simple with yet is only heard in informal American English.
The present simple does not express that something is still pending up to now: haven't finished.
After have you need the participle: finished.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the present perfect or the past simple.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the note in the card: questions with When or What time always take the past simple, because they ask about a specific moment. The clue is When at the beginning. That is why the question has did + subject + infinitive: When did you start? The verb goes back to the base form start, since did marks the past.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: When requires the past simple: did + infinitive.

errores_previstos.explicacion: When asks about a specific moment and does not allow the present perfect.
After did the verb is in the infinitive: did you start.
The auxiliary did and the inversion are missing: When did you start?

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the present perfect or the past simple.
ejercicios.frase: My brother ___ (just / call) me. He's on his way.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the present perfect table: just is one of its typical words and expresses something that has only now happened with an effect in the present. The clue is just together with the second sentence, He's on his way, which shows the present result of the call. That is why it is has just called, with just between the auxiliary and the participle. In American English you also hear My brother just called me, in the past simple, but the card practises the British standard.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Just with a present result: present perfect.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi hermano me acaba de llamar. Está de camino.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Just goes between the auxiliary and the participle: has just called.
With my brother (he) the auxiliary is has.
Just does not go before the auxiliary but after it: has just called.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: a past date (in 2019) requires the past simple. The clue is in 2019, a year that is already over. The mistake is typical of learners who translate “he conocido” with the present perfect: in English, as soon as a date appears, the tense is the past simple. Met is the irregular past of meet, which here means “to get to know someone for the first time”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: In 2019 is finished time: past simple.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the present perfect does not combine with a past date like in 2019.
Have has been removed but the verb has been left in the present; the past of meet is met.
Besides using the wrong tense, after have you would need the participle met.

ejercicios.frase: What time have you got up this morning?
respuestas: What time did you get up this morning?
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the note in the card about questions with What time, which always take the past simple because they ask about a specific moment. The clue is What time, reinforced by this morning: if the morning is already over, it is a finished moment. That is why the form is did you get up, with the verb get up in the infinitive after did. In the Spanish of Spain we say “¿a qué hora te has levantado?”, and that is where the mistake comes from.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: What time asks about a specific moment: past simple.
ejercicios.traduccion: ¿A qué hora te levantaste esta mañana?

errores_previstos.respuesta: What time have you got up this morning?
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: What time requires the past simple.

errores_previstos.respuesta: What time did you got up this morning?
errores_previstos.explicacion: After did the verb is in the infinitive: get up.

errores_previstos.respuesta: What time you got up this morning?
errores_previstos.explicacion: The question needs the auxiliary did before the subject.

ejercicios.frase: She has left the office an hour ago.
respuestas: She left the office an hour ago.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the table: ago goes with the past simple. The clue is an hour ago: even though very little time has passed, ago turns it into a specific, finished moment. That is why has left becomes left, the past of leave. This case shows the central idea of the card: what matters is not whether it is recent, but whether the moment is closed.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With ago you use the past simple, not the present perfect.
ejercicios.traduccion: Salió de la oficina hace una hora.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She has left the office an hour ago.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the present perfect is not used with ago.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She leaved the office an hour ago.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Leave is irregular: its past form is left.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She has left the office since an hour.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Since needs a starting point, not a duration, and the meaning also changes; just use left with ago.

ejercicios.enunciado: Rewrite the sentence adding “last summer” at the end and changing the tense.
respuestas: I went to Lisbon last summer.
I was in Lisbon last summer.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the first note in the list: experience with no date in the present perfect (I've visited Japan twice), but with a date in the past simple (I visited Japan in 2018). When you add last summer, a finished time, the present perfect has to become the past simple. The clue is in the form: have been to becomes went to, the past of go, which is the natural choice for a trip. I was in Lisbon last summer is also correct: was in is the past of be in, and corresponds to the have been of the original sentence.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: When you add a finished moment, the present perfect becomes the past simple (have been → went / was).
ejercicios.traduccion: Fui a Lisboa el verano pasado.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I have been to Lisbon last summer.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Last summer has been added but the tense has not been changed: with a finished time you need the past simple.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I was been to Lisbon last summer.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Mixed forms: the past of have been to a place is went to (or was in).

errores_previstos.respuesta: I went in Lisbon last summer.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With verbs of movement like go the destination is introduced with to: went to Lisbon.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the present perfect table: never expresses an experience in your whole life up to now. The clue for the word order is that never goes between the auxiliary and the participle: have + never + tried. That is why the order is I have never tried sushi. Try here means “to taste” (a food).

errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of an order with the object in the middle: in English the object sushi goes after the participle, and never between have and tried.
Never cannot go after the participle; it goes between have and tried.
If never goes at the beginning, English requires inversion (Never have I tried…), an emphatic and formal construction; with this order the sentence is incorrect.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the note in the card: questions with When always take the past simple. The clue is the word when, which goes at the beginning, and the auxiliary did, which marks the past. The order is When + did + subject + infinitive: when did they arrive. The verb arrive stays in the base form, without -ed, because did already shows the past.

errores_previstos.explicacion: In the question the auxiliary did goes before the subject: when did they.
The subject goes between did and the verb: did they arrive.
In English the question word when goes at the beginning of the question.

descripcion_larga_es: Choosing between the present perfect and the past simple depends on whether the time we are talking about is finished (yesterday, in 2019, ago) or continues up to now or is not specified (ever, yet, since). It is one of the most frequent decisions when talking about the past. Speakers from Spain find it hard because they use the pretérito perfecto for recent events (“esta mañana he ido”), and English does not follow that criterion.

contexto.que_es: It is the contrast between two tenses that Spanish does not divide up in the same way. The past simple (I went, did you go?) places the action in a finished past time; the present perfect (I have gone, have you been?) connects it with the present: experiences with no date, periods that are still open or present results. The key is not whether it was recent, but whether the period is closed.
contexto.por_que_importa: When telling experiences or news you have to choose one of the two in almost every sentence. Using the present perfect with a date (“I have met him in 2019”) is a very typical mistake of speakers from Spain that a native speaker notices at once. Moreover, the choice changes the meaning: Shakespeare wrote versus My sister has written indicates whether the person can go on writing.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: Past simple with yesterday, last week, ago, in 2019, when I was a child and in questions with When or What time. Present perfect with ever, never, already, yet, just, so far, since and for, and for experiences with no date. It is common to start in the present perfect (Have you seen it?) and move to the past simple when giving details (Yes, I saw it on Saturday).
